title: Cells: The Basic Units of Life

standard_text: The cell theory; the microscope and magnification; the structure and functions of the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, vacuole and cell wall; differences between plant and animal cells; movement of substances by diffusion, osmosis and active transport. key_big: All living things are made of cells.

body_html:
How to think about it

The cell theory states that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells. Organelles have special functions: the nucleus controls the cell, mitochondria carry out respiration, ribosomes make proteins, and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; animal cells do not. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration; osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane; active transport uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient.

Example

Which organelle releases energy from food?

The powerhouse of the cell

Answer: the mitochondrion

Example

Image 20 mm, real size 0,02 mm. Magnification?

image ÷ actual

Answer: × 1 000

Common mistakes

  • Thinking animal cells have cell walls.
  • Thinking osmosis is the movement of salt.
  • Measuring the image and real size in different units.

faq.q: Why do plant cells not burst in pure water?
faq.a: The strong cell wall stops them from swelling too much.

faq.q: What does a light microscope show that the eye cannot?
faq.a: Cells and some organelles, such as the nucleus, magnified up to about 1 000 times.

items.q: What is active transport?
c: movement against a concentration gradient using ATP and carrier proteins
items.e: Carrier proteins change shape.

items.q: Which process moves large particles out of a cell in vesicles?
items.e: Vesicles fuse with the membrane to release their contents.

items.q: Why can oxygen diffuse straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Ions need channel proteins.

items.q: Why is a virus not considered a living cell?
c: it has no cytoplasm or ribosomes and can only replicate inside a host cell
items.e: Viruses are acellular.

items.q: How does sodium–glucose co-transport absorb glucose in the ileum?
c: Na⁺ diffuses into the cell down its gradient, carrying glucose with it
glucose is pumped out by ATP
items.e: The gradient is set up by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

items.q: Which organelle makes proteins?
items.e: Ribosomes are on the rough ER and free in the cytoplasm.

items.q: In a photograph a palisade cell is 250 mm long. The magnification is ×5 000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 250 mm ÷ 5 000 = 0,0500 mm = 50,0 µm.

items.q: What is active transport?
c: movement against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP
movement down a gradient with no energy
items.e: Root hair cells take up mineral ions this way.

items.q: What is the function of the Golgi apparatus?
c: modifying and packaging proteins and lipids into vesicles
items.e: It also makes lysosomes.

items.q: What is the function of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
items.e: It has no ribosomes.

items.q: What is the main function of chromoplasts?
c: giving colour to fruits and flowers
the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Chromoplasts: giving colour to fruits and flowers.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for storing starch, oils and proteins?
items.e: Leucoplasts: storing starch, oils and proteins.

How does a white blood cell take in a bacterium?
items.e: The membrane surrounds the particle.

items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 20 000 µm = 20,0 mm.

items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 25,0 mm ÷ 5 000 = 0,00500 mm = 5,00 µm.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for giving colour to fruits and flowers?
items.e: Chromoplasts: giving colour to fruits and flowers.

items.q: A scale bar 30 mm long represents 5 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
What is the evidence that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
c: they are bigger than the nucleus
they are found in every prokaryote
they have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and a double membrane
items.e: This is the endosymbiotic theory.

items.q: A cheek cell is 80,0 µm long. Its image is 16,0 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
items.e: Change mm to µm: 16 000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×200.

items.q: What is the main function of mitochondria?
c: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: What is a metacentric chromosome?
c: one with the centromere at the end
one with the centromere in the middle and two equal arms
items.e: Telocentric chromosomes have a terminal centromere.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
c: a lipid bilayer in which proteins float, with the lipid able to move sideways
items.e: Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).

items.q: What is the main function of rough endoplasmic reticulum?
items.e: Rough endoplasmic reticulum: making and secreting proteins.

items.q: What does the 'S' in 70S ribosome stand for?
c: the Svedberg unit, a measure of sedimentation
items.e: It depends on size and shape.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making and secreting proteins?
items.e: Rough endoplasmic reticulum: making and secreting proteins.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for digesting materials with hydrolytic enzymes?
items.e: Lysosomes: digesting materials with hydrolytic enzymes.

items.q: What are the stacks of thylakoids in a chloroplast called?
items.e: The fluid around them is the stroma.

items.q: What is the main function of vacuole?
c: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid
the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Vacuole: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid.

items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 12,0 mm ÷ 200 = 0,0600 mm = 60,0 µm.

items.q: What is the main function of Golgi apparatus?
c: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids
items.e: Golgi apparatus: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

items.q: Who explained that all cells arise from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula-e cellula)?
items.e: This completed the cell theory.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)?
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: What is the main function of leucoplasts?
c: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Leucoplasts: storing starch, oils and proteins.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making lipids and steroid hormones?
items.e: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: making lipids and steroid hormones.

items.q: What is the main function of centrioles?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Centrioles: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia.

items.e: Centrioles: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia.

items.q: What is the shape of the cilia and flagella axoneme in cross-section?
items.e: Nine outer doublets and two central singlets.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of protein synthesis?
items.e: Ribosomes: the site of protein synthesis.

items.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
items.e: Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP.

items.q: Which cells contain mitochondria?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: A chloroplast is 5,00 µm long. Its image is 100 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
items.e: Change mm to µm: 100 000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×20 000.

items.q: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
c: sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
items.e: The centromeres divide.

items.q: What does a scanning electron microscope produce?
c: a colour image of living cells
items.e: Its resolution is lower than a TEM.

items.q: Daniel is labelling a cell model. What is the main job of the chloroplasts?
c: A stiff outer layer that supports and protects a plant cell
A jelly-like fluid that holds the other parts
Capture sunlight to make food (sugar) by photosynthesis
items.e: The chloroplasts capture sunlight to make food (sugar) by photosynthesis.

items.q: Which cells contain a cell membrane?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: What are the ribosomes of prokaryotes?
items.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts also have 70S ribosomes.

items.q: Bongani is labelling a cell model. What is the main job of the mitochondria?
c: Controls the cell's activities and holds the genetic information (DNA)
Release energy from food (sugar) for the cell to use
Capture sunlight to make food (sugar) by photosynthesis
items.e: The mitochondria release energy from food (sugar) for the cell to use.

items.q: What do lysosomes contain?
items.e: They digest worn-out organelles and pathogens.

items.q: Liam is labelling a cell model. What is the main job of the cell wall?
c: A stiff outer layer that supports and protects a plant cell
Release energy from food (sugar) for the cell to use
Capture sunlight to make food (sugar) by photosynthesis
items.e: The cell wall a stiff outer layer that supports and protects a plant cell.

items.q: What is resolution?
c: how much bigger the image is
the ability to distinguish two points that are close together
items.e: Magnification without resolution gives a blurred image.

items.q: In ultracentrifugation, which organelle forms the first pellet?
items.e: The heaviest organelles settle at the lowest speed.

items.q: Chloe is labelling a cell model. What is the main job of the nucleus?
c: Controls the cell's activities and holds the genetic information (DNA)
Controls what enters and leaves the cell
A stiff outer layer that supports and protects a plant cell
items.e: The nucleus controls the cell's activities and holds the genetic information (DNA).

items.q: Which cells contain a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: Which cells contain cytoplasm?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: Which cells contain chloroplasts?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: Lungile is labelling a cell model. What is the main job of the vacuole?
c: A stiff outer layer that supports and protects a plant cell
Release energy from food (sugar) for the cell to use
A jelly-like fluid that holds the other parts
items.e: The vacuole stores water and other materials.

items.q: Which cells contain a nucleus?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: What does cholesterol do in a cell membrane?
c: it reduces fluidity and makes the membrane more stable
items.e: It sits between the phospholipids.

items.q: Which statement compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells correctly?
c: only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
items.e: Both have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −700 kPa and the sucrose solution has −600 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from the sucrose solution to a potato cell
from a potato cell to the sucrose solution
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −400 kPa and cell B has −250 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell B to cell A
from cell A to cell B
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer in water?
c: their phosphate heads are hydrophilic and their fatty acid tails are hydrophobic
items.e: Tails face inwards away from water.

items.q: What is diffusion?
c: net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
movement against a concentration gradient using ATP
movement of large particles in vesicles
items.e: Diffusion is passive.

items.q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What happens?
c: water leaves and the cell becomes plasmolysed
the cell takes in salt by osmosis
water enters and the cell bursts
items.e: The membrane pulls away from the cell wall.

items.q: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens?
c: water leaves and the cell shrinks
water enters by osmosis and the cell may burst
the cell wall stops it bursting
items.e: Animal cells have no cell wall.

items.q: What is osmosis?
c: net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution
movement of any particle from high to low concentration
movement of salt across a membrane
items.e: Water moves towards the higher solute concentration.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −500 kPa and cell Y has −100 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell Y to cell X
from cell X to cell Y
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Which molecule can diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Small, non-polar molecules pass easily.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −700 kPa and the sucrose solution has −250 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−250 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −300 kPa and cell Y has −800 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−300 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −1 200 kPa and cell B has −400 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−400 kPa) is higher.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Glucose and ions often need protein channels.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model?
c: a layer of DNA around the cell
a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that can move within it
items.e: Proteins float in a fluid bilayer.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −300 kPa and cell B has −800 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−300 kPa) is higher.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −800 kPa and the salt solution has −500 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−500 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Why must cells stay small?
c: as a cell grows, its surface area to volume ratio falls, so exchange becomes too slow
items.e: Volume grows faster than surface area.

items.q: How do prokaryotic cells divide?
items.e: The circular DNA and plasmids are copied first.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement of molecules through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Down a concentration gradient.
